problems.1: Wholesale forecasts are the least accurate, and the data barely shape them
problems.2: Adding data makes some totals less certain, sometimes absurdly so
problems.3: Uncertainty ranges are generally too wide
problems.4: Utilization is confidently wrong in Food and Autos
problems.5: Hotels do not match official employment or prices
problems.6: Oil and gas is weak across the board
problems.7: Cost pass-through and normal markup come from group averages, not from each firm's own data
problems.8: Order-flow and lead-time totals are mostly assumed
problems.9: Good scores against later estimates may partly be the model agreeing with itself
problems.10: Large parts of the model have no outside check

fixes.label: 1A
fixes.title: Keep the best of three Wholesale fits
fixes.fix: Fit Wholesale three times at each as-of date with different random numbers and keep the fit that best predicts observations held back from fitting. On the previous world this stopped Wholesale's capacity from jumping between runs (from about 27% to 7% at the same month) and halved its error against the truth, but it was never adopted. Wholesale's large gap between runs here looks like the same problem.
fixes.test: Three Wholesale fits per date with a held-out check, then filters, on two random-number sets; Wholesale's gap on Forecasts against later estimates should fall well below 5.9% and its hit rate should come down toward 90/100.

fixes.label: 1B
fixes.title: Fit Wholesale without sector inventory readings
fixes.fix: Fit Wholesale's parameters without the whole-sector inventory readings and use those readings only in the monthly filter, as was done for Oil and gas's official stock readings. On the previous world the model's Wholesale stock ran about 65% above these readings whatever was tried, so in fitting they may be bending Wholesale's other parameters, and its volumes with them, to reconcile a stock level the rest of its data do not support; the same change for Oil and gas cut its forecast gap from 13.6% to 5.7%.
fixes.test: Four-date Wholesale fits and filters on two random-number sets; Wholesale's gap on Forecasts against later estimates should fall well below 5.9% with its sector-inventory readings on Observations against the model no worse.

fixes.label: 1C
fixes.title: Add company gross margins for tracked wholesalers
fixes.fix: Add the cost of goods sold that wholesale companies report each quarter to their observations. A wholesaler's unit cost is mostly what it pays for goods, which these reports show directly, so the model could separate cost from margin firm by firm instead of leaning on the sector's margin index and group averages; its pass-through parameter is now learned for no Wholesale firm.
fixes.test: Rebuild the world with the new reports and run four-date Wholesale fits and filters; Wholesale's stricter informative share and its pass-through on What the data pin down should rise, and its forecast gap should fall.

fixes.label: 1D
fixes.title: Give Wholesale a monthly volume reading
fixes.fix: Add a monthly reading of how much goods tracked wholesalers move, such as freight or warehouse activity counts. Today Wholesale's data are quarterly sales, stock, yearly capacity and a monthly margin index, so nothing monthly bears on volume and output, shipments and orders are left to the equations.
fixes.test: Rebuild the world with the new reading and run four-date Wholesale fits and filters; Wholesale's output, shipments and order book on What the data pin down should fall below 0.8 and its forecast gap should shrink.

fixes.label: 2A
fixes.title: Mark negligible quantities instead of dividing
fixes.fix: Where a quantity is almost always zero, as lost demand is in Hospitals and Airlines, report it as negligible rather than as a ratio of two tiny spreads, and measure the other ratios from the copies' total spread over the history. Tested on the previous world, this removed Hospitals', Hotels' and Airlines' huge lost-demand ratios and cut the unsettled cells from 17 to 11, and a rerun showed the old ratios were noise; it was never adopted.
fixes.test: Recompute What the data pin down from this world's runs; Hospitals' 2810 and Airlines' 8.94 lost demand should disappear from the unsettled list and the count of cells above 1.2 should fall well below 26.

fixes.label: 2B
fixes.title: Let stocked-out copies recover their inventory
fixes.fix: Remove the filter rule that stops adjusting a simulated copy's finished stock for good once it has run out with orders late. Tested on the previous world for another reason, it had a large side effect: overdue orders in Oil and gas and Machinery stopped running away, and the error against the truth fell from 0.108 to 0.074. The extreme overdue and phantom order ratios in Oil and gas look like the same runaway copies.
fixes.test: A four-date backtest on two random-number sets; Oil and gas overdue orders, phantom orders and finished inventory on What the data pin down should fall from 18.60, 11.70 and 1.90 to near or below 1.

fixes.label: 2C
fixes.title: Use a filter update that cannot widen
fixes.fix: Replace the filter's random perturbation of each reading with the deterministic form of the same update, which can only narrow the copies' spread. With 100 copies, the random perturbation and chance links between a reading and unrelated quantities can push copies apart; an earlier test showed Retail's copies spreading about three times wider with data and no runaway copies to blame.
fixes.test: Four-date backtests on two random-number sets; the cells above 1.2 on What the data pin down, especially Retail's and Machinery's new orders, should fall to 1 or below, with Observations against the model no worse.

fixes.label: 2D
fixes.title: Let sector-wide readings move only what they measure
fixes.fix: Extend the rule just adopted for Wholesale's margin index, which may now change only unit cost and markup, to the other whole-sector readings such as official production, sales and inventories: each may move only the quantities it measures and their direct inputs. For Wholesale this cut the error against the truth by about a quarter, because chance links in the ensemble had let the index push capacity and stock around.
fixes.test: A four-date backtest; unsettled cells on What the data pin down, especially Retail's order totals and Housing's and Machinery's new orders, should fall below 1.2 with official-statistic agreement no worse.

fixes.label: 3A
fixes.title: Score observations before the model uses them
fixes.fix: On Observations against the model, compare each reading with the model's range from just before that reading was used, not after. A range that has already been pulled toward the reading will catch it too easily and look close to it, which would explain 96/100 in range; scoring the forecast made one step earlier is the honest test of whether the assumed noise is too large.
fixes.test: Rerun the filters at the four dates keeping the before-update ranges and rebuild the page; the overall rate on Observations against the model should move toward 90/100 and closeness toward 41%, or, if it stays at 96, the noise settings are the cause.

fixes.label: 3B
fixes.title: Recalibrate the range widening on the newest worlds
fixes.fix: Reset the factors that widen every published range, per quantity and horizon, using backtests of the current model on the two newest synthetic worlds instead of the older world they were set on. Many changes since then, such as the filter's order-level adjustments and the treatment of official statistics, have made the model's own ranges wider; on an earlier world per-quantity factors set on older worlds overshot, which is why newer worlds are needed.
fixes.test: Four-date backtests of the current model on two recent worlds to set the factors, then this world's ranges rebuilt; the overall rate on Forecasts against later estimates should fall from 97/100 toward 90/100 and fewer sectors should read wider than needed.

fixes.label: 3C
fixes.title: Widen ranges less where data pin a quantity
fixes.fix: Scale the extra widening of each sector total by how much the data narrow it: little or none where a quantity is pinned, the full amount where it comes mostly from the model. The widening stands in for uncertainty the copies do not carry, such as parameters on weakly learned ridges, and that matters for model-driven totals, not for output or capacity that the data already settle.
fixes.test: Rebuild the ranges from this world's runs and check them against the truth on two earlier worlds; on Forecasts against later estimates pinned quantities should drop from about 99/100 toward 90/100 without model-driven ones falling below 85/100.

fixes.label: 4A
fixes.title: Let official utilization size Food's and Autos' untracked firms
fixes.fix: During fitting, let the official utilization rate, not just official production, set the capacity of Food's and Autos' untracked firms. On the previous world this fixed Steel's utilization (55/100 to 99/100) but hurt Machinery, whose misses came from tracked firms instead, so it should be tried only where production already agrees and utilization does not, as in Food and Autos.
fixes.test: Four-date Food and Autos fits and filters on two random-number sets; their utilization rows on Sector totals against official statistics should rise above 90/100 with production no worse.

fixes.label: 4B
fixes.title: Check how utilization is compared with the official figure
fixes.fix: Check step by step how Food's and Autos' utilization is built from firms and compared with the official rate: which firms count, whether it is weighted by capacity or output, and how untracked firms enter. A similar check of Retail sales on the previous world found two real mismatches, one in units and one in timing, and fixing them took Retail from 83/100 to 97/100.
fixes.test: Fix any mismatch found and rerun Food and Autos at four dates; their utilization rows on Sector totals against official statistics should agree, with the gap under 0.5%.

fixes.label: 4C
fixes.title: Keep the best of three Food and Autos fits
fixes.fix: Fit Food and Autos three times at each as-of date and keep the fit that best predicts held-back observations. Choosing among fits this way helped Machinery, Wholesale and Oil and gas on the previous world, and a confident but wrong capacity level is what one unlucky fit would produce.
fixes.test: Three fits per date for Food and Autos with a held-out check, then filters; their utilization rows on Sector totals against official statistics should rise above 90/100.

fixes.label: 5A
fixes.title: Record hotel bookings in the month observed
fixes.fix: In the service sectors, write the filter's correction to advance bookings into the month that was observed rather than the month after. Tested on the previous world, this settled Hotels' lost demand and halved Hotels' error against the truth, with Observations against the model holding or improving, but it was never adopted. A booking correction that lands a month late would leave occupancy, staffing and room rates out of step.
fixes.test: Four-date filters of Hotels, Hospitals and Airlines with those sectors refitted; Hotels' load factor and lead time on What the data pin down should fall below 1.2 and its employee and lodging-price rows on Sector totals against official statistics should rise.

fixes.label: 5B
fixes.title: Anchor untracked hotels to official employment
fixes.fix: During fitting, set the overall size of the hotels the model does not track individually from the official accommodation employment figure, much as other sectors' untracked firms are anchored to official production. Hotels have no official output figure to anchor to, only employment and lodging prices, so their untracked part is sized from yearly establishment employment alone, and a size or staffing ratio that is off would show as a steady gap against monthly official employment.
fixes.test: Four-date Hotels fits on two random-number sets; accommodation employment on Sector totals against official statistics should rise from 83/100 with the 2.1% gap roughly halved.

fixes.label: 5C
fixes.title: Add advance-booking readings for Hotels
fixes.fix: Give tracked hotel companies a quarterly reading of rooms already booked for coming months. On the previous world, adding such readings halved Hotels' error against the truth even though the order book itself stayed partly model-driven, which suggests occupancy and staffing would follow the data better.
fixes.test: Rebuild the world with the readings and run four-date Hotels fits and filters; Hotels on Observations against the model and its employee row on Sector totals against official statistics should rise, and load factor should fall below 1.2.

fixes.label: 5D
fixes.title: Let hotel staffing per room drift over time
fixes.fix: Let the number of workers per unit of hotel output change slowly over the years instead of staying fixed. If staffing practice shifts, a fixed ratio would make the model's employment drift away from the official figure even when occupancy is right.
fixes.test: Four-date Hotels fits on two random-number sets; accommodation employment on Sector totals against official statistics should rise from 83/100 without Hotels' Observations against the model getting worse.

fixes.label: 6A
fixes.title: Fit Oil and gas without official stock readings
fixes.fix: Fit Oil and gas without the official petroleum stock readings and use them only in the monthly filter. On the previous world this took Oil and gas on Forecasts against later estimates from 76/100 with a 13.6% gap to 89/100 with 5.7%, settled finished inventory, and cut its error against the truth from 0.28 to 0.11, but it was one run on one set of random numbers and was never adopted.
fixes.test: Four-date Oil and gas fits and filters on two random-number sets; its gap on Forecasts against later estimates should fall well below 5.6% and finished inventory and order book on What the data pin down below 1.2.

fixes.label: 6B
fixes.title: Keep the best held-out Oil and gas fit
fixes.fix: Fit Oil and gas three times at each date, keep the fit that best predicts held-back observations, then finish it on all the data starting from that fit rather than refitting from scratch. On the previous world the chosen held-out fits themselves gave 96/100 with a 3.3% gap, but refitting from scratch on all data landed somewhere else and lost the gain.
fixes.test: Three Oil and gas fits per date with a held-out check and a warm-started finish, then filters; its gap on Forecasts against later estimates should fall below 4% and vary less between dates.

fixes.label: 6C
fixes.title: Give Oil and gas a short order pipeline
fixes.fix: Treat Oil and gas as a sector that produces to flow: hold its order book and lead time to a short fixed length instead of estimating them. Its order book, overdue and phantom orders carry the most unsettled totals in the model, yet no Oil and gas reading measures orders, so these parts add room to wander without adding information.
fixes.test: Four-date Oil and gas fits and filters; its order-side cells on What the data pin down should stop being unsettled and its forecast gap should fall without its official production and utilization rows getting worse.

fixes.label: 7A
fixes.title: Add gross margins to company reports
fixes.fix: Add the cost of goods sold, or gross margin, to tracked companies' quarterly reports in every sector that publishes them. Today nothing measures a firm's unit cost directly, so cost pass-through and normal markup can only be guessed from price and revenue, and by the stricter measure they are learned for about one firm in ten.
fixes.test: Rebuild the world with the new figures and run four-date backtests on two random-number sets; the stricter informative share for pass-through and markup on What the data pin down should rise well above 12 and 11 of 115, and unit cost's gap on Forecasts against later estimates should fall.

fixes.label: 7B
fixes.title: Add official input-cost indexes by sector
fixes.fix: Give each sector an official index of what it pays for its inputs, such as producer price indexes for the materials it buys. Pass-through measures how much of an input-cost change reaches a firm's unit cost; with the cost change itself observed, firms' price movements could reveal their own pass-through rather than the group's.
fixes.test: Rebuild the world with the indexes and run a four-date backtest; w on What the data pin down (by parameter) should no longer be the least-informed parameter in most sectors, and unit cost's gap should shrink.

fixes.label: 7C
fixes.title: Share pass-through and markup where data are thin
fixes.fix: In sectors where observations held back from fitting are predicted as well or better, use one pass-through and one markup for the whole sector instead of one per firm. This would stop reporting parameters the data cannot set, but a similar test for other parameters only flattered the count and made accuracy worse, so it is a long shot.
fixes.test: A held-out check per sector to choose, then a four-date backtest; the stricter informative share should rise with unit cost's and price's gaps on Forecasts against later estimates no worse.

fixes.label: 8A
fixes.title: Add materials inventories in four sectors
fixes.fix: Add official monthly materials inventories for Food, Chemicals, Steel and Autos only. On an earlier world such readings pinned input inventory in exactly these four sectors (spread ratios 0.18-0.76 from about 1) and cut its error against the truth by a third; Oil and gas and Housing, where they did not help and one fit blew up, are left out this time.
fixes.test: Rebuild the world and run four-date backtests on two random-number sets; input inventory on What the data pin down should fall below 0.8 in those four sectors with no sector getting worse.

fixes.label: 8B
fixes.title: Add lead-time readings in more sectors
fixes.fix: Add delivery lead-time readings, such as supplier-delivery survey answers or company-reported lead times, for sectors that now have none, including Wholesale, Data centers, Hospitals and Airlines. Lead time has the largest forecast gap of any quantity and is model-driven in four sectors, all of them sectors without any lead-time reading.
fixes.test: Rebuild the world and run a four-date backtest; lead time on What the data pin down should fall below 0.8 in those sectors and its gap on Forecasts against later estimates should fall from 7.0%.

fixes.label: 8C
fixes.title: Add signed leases and bookings to the order data
fixes.fix: Add data-center leases signed but not yet started and hotel and airline advance bookings, all tried together on an earlier world. That test pinned Data centers' order book (0.88 to 0.74) and clearly improved accuracy where the data were added, but was never adopted; Data centers' order totals here are entirely model-driven.
fixes.test: Rebuild the world and run a four-date backtest; Data centers' order book, shipments and lead time on What the data pin down should fall below 0.8.

fixes.label: 9A
fixes.title: Check forecasts against later observations
fixes.fix: Add a check of each forecast against the readings that arrived after its as-of date, which involves no later estimate by the model. Tested on the previous world, it told a different story from the model grading itself, Hospitals 84/100 against 99/100, and exposed misses the self-check hid, but it was never adopted.
fixes.test: Compute the new check from this world's four runs; Hospitals' and Wholesale's scores on it should differ from Forecasts against later estimates where the model grades itself.

fixes.label: 9B
fixes.title: Show data-informed and model-only scores side by side
fixes.fix: On Forecasts against later estimates, show the hit rate and gap separately for values the data inform and values that come mostly from the model. Tested on the previous world, this put nearly all input inventory in the model-only column and showed which sectors' data-informed ranges were too narrow, so small gaps from model-driven values can no longer pass for accuracy.
fixes.test: Rebuild the page from this world's runs; Hospitals' model-driven totals should appear only in the model-only column and the data-informed column should give its own hit rate and gap.

fixes.label: 9C
fixes.title: Show a simple baseline beside each score
fixes.fix: Next to each sector's forecast gap, show the gap a naive forecast would have, such as carrying the last estimate forward. A model-driven sector whose forecasts barely move will score well against its own later estimates, and the baseline makes that visible.
fixes.test: Rebuild Forecasts against later estimates from this world's runs; Hospitals' 0.6% gap should be shown beside a baseline gap, revealing whether it beats doing nothing.

fixes.label: 10A
fixes.title: Add check-only official sales for Wholesale
fixes.fix: Show the official monthly wholesale sales figure beside the model's Wholesale sales as a check the model never uses. Tested on the previous world it gave Wholesale its first outside test, which Wholesale failed, a useful finding that was never adopted.
fixes.test: Rebuild the world and filter Wholesale at four dates; Sector totals against official statistics should gain a Wholesale row.

fixes.label: 10B
fixes.title: Add a check-only statistic for Data centers
fixes.fix: Compare Data centers' total capacity in use with an outside figure the model never uses, such as published estimates of data-center electricity use or construction spending. Data centers have no official statistic at all, so today the reader has only the model's own consistency to go on.
fixes.test: Rebuild the world with the new series and filter Data centers at four dates; Sector totals against official statistics should gain a Data centers row and say whether it agrees.

fixes.label: 10C
fixes.title: Add check-only housing starts and sales
fixes.fix: Compare Housing's new orders and order book with official new-home sales and housing starts, without letting the model pull toward them. Using new-orders statistics as inputs made Housing less accurate on an earlier world, but as checks only they give Housing an outside test beyond completions.
fixes.test: Rebuild the world and filter Housing at four dates; Sector totals against official statistics should gain Housing rows for starts or sales and say whether they agree.
